titre: The Moment You Are Nothing Anymore
accroche: During a rite of passage, there is a phase in which you have no social status at all, neither the old one nor the new one.
contenu_vulgarise:
Before an initiation ceremony, an adolescent is a child. Afterward, he is an adult. But during? In a great many societies, initiates go through a phase in which they are officially neither: they are isolated, stripped of their names, sometimes dressed so as to erase their previous identity. This suspended moment was named and theorized as early as 1909 by the French ethnographer Arnold van Gennep, in *Les Rites de passage* (*The Rites of Passage*).

## Three Stages, One Hinge

Van Gennep divides every rite of passage (birth, puberty, marriage, funerals) into three sequences: separation, which detaches the individual from his former status; the margin (or liminality, from the Latin *limen*, the threshold), during which he belongs to no stable category; and incorporation, which installs him in his new status, recognized by the group. Van Gennep takes care to specify that the three never carry the same weight: separation dominates funerals, incorporation marriage. The margin, for its part, “can constitute an important section, for example in pregnancy, betrothal, initiation, or be reduced to a minimum” elsewhere. It is this phase, when it stretches out, that the British anthropologist Victor Turner took up and deepened sixty years later, based on the fieldwork he carried out between 1950 and 1954 among the Ndembu of Northern Rhodesia, present-day Zambia.

Turner, in *The Ritual Process* (1969, translated into French as *Le Phénomène rituel*), shows that this liminal phase is not a mere empty in-between: it produces its own temporary social order, which Turner calls *communitas*. It is a provisional equality among initiates, stripped together of their ordinary statuses, which momentarily erases the hierarchies of the world before and after. It is precisely because they are nothing, socially, that initiates can, for the length of the rite, be equal to one another.

## What This Shifts

The interest of liminality extends beyond religious rites. Turner extends it to any situation in which a person or a group finds itself “between” two recognized social structures: the newcomer not yet integrated, the mourning period before the status of widower or widow is officially recognized, the waiting zone of an exam or competitive entrance exam, where you are no longer a student but have not yet passed. These moments share a trait: the temporary absence of status is often experienced there as more intense, more fraternal, or more destabilizing than the stable states around it.

What Turner's theory shifts is the idea that social blur must always be a problem to be solved as quickly as possible. In many societies, it is organized instead with great care, through precise and repeated rites, because it may be the only condition in which something can truly change status without anyone contesting the change once it is made.

repere.texte: In The Ritual Process (1969), drawn from the fieldwork he carried out from 1950 to 1954 among the Ndembu of present-day Zambia, Victor Turner takes up and extends the three-phase model proposed sixty years earlier by Arnold van Gennep in The Rites of Passage (1909).
repere.source: Victor Turner, The Ritual Process, 1969; Arnold van Gennep, The Rites of Passage (Les Rites de passage), 1909

carte.punch: During the rite, you are officially nothing.
carte.idee: Van Gennep, then Turner, showed that every rite of passage goes through a phase in which the individual no longer has the old status and does not yet have the new one, an in-between that societies organize with care rather than seeing it as a problem to be solved quickly.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Biographical landmarks and the place of his work in French ethnography.

quiz.question: What is meant by “communitas” in Victor Turner's work?
choix: The name of the Ndembu village where Turner carried out his fieldwork
The assembly of elders that leads the ritual
The set of separation rites that open the ceremony
The provisional equality among initiates during the liminal phase
quiz.explication: By “communitas,” Turner means the egalitarian, provisional bond that unites initiates during the liminal phase, when they are stripped together of their ordinary social statuses, before regaining a distinct place in the structure.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Arnold van Gennep divide every rite of passage in 1909?
choix: Into three sequences: separation, margin (or liminality), then incorporation
Into only two moments: before and after the ceremony
Into four ritual stages, specific to each society studied
Into a single continuous phase, with no identifiable break
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Van Gennep divides every rite of passage into three sequences: separation, which detaches from the former status, the margin, where one belongs to no stable category, and incorporation, which installs the new status.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to van Gennep himself, does the margin phase always occupy the same place in a rite of passage?
choix: Yes: it always makes up the majority of ritual time, whatever the rite
No: it has disappeared entirely from the funeral rites van Gennep studied
No: it can dominate, for example, initiation, but be reduced to a minimum elsewhere
Yes: van Gennep fixes its length at exactly one third of the ceremony
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Van Gennep specifies that the three sequences never carry the same weight: the margin can constitute an important section, for example in initiation, or be reduced to a minimum depending on the rite.

quiz_supplementaire.question: To what situations does Turner extend the idea of liminality beyond religious rites?
choix: Only to the funeral rites studied among the Ndembu
Any situation between two recognized social structures, such as an exam or mourning
Only to twentieth-century Western wedding ceremonies
To initiation rites practiced exclusively in southern Africa
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Turner extends liminality to any situation in which a person or a group finds itself between two recognized social structures: the newcomer not yet integrated, mourning before the status of widower, an exam.
